english: The serpent was stealing the men's cows. It had three heads. It led them down into a rock. Now the third, the youngest, Hyudhsmos, took a heavy (club). He climbed the rock and roared: 'Serpent, give them to me.' The serpent growled; the third struck its three heads. He killed the serpent and drove out them and the (?) . Then the rock trembled. The men gave him the first share of the herd. The third said: 'Give it to the women; I want a name.'

Dusmenes stood over him on the ground of this (?) place, and Hsntyokleves too. Dusmenes said: 'Hsntyokleves, do not kill me. I give you ten cows and horses.' Hsntyokleves said: 'Swear an oath.' Then Dusmenes raised his hand toward the sky: 'Father Sky, hear me. If I deceive him, strike me.' Then the two men (set/brought back?) the oath and the stall. Dusmenes led ten horses to him at dawn and did not deceive him. The oath stood and was never broken.
uncertain: first clause: dʰǵʰémi ḱéyo h₁ésmi upér — who stood over whom unclear

english: The youths wore wolf skins. They lived in the hills(?) and ate raw meat. Their teeth were sharp. The snow on the hills was deep. Their mothers did not recognize them. For three years they seized the strangers' cows. They brought them (as price/gift) to their own fathers. The fathers followed: 'Now you are men, you are not wolves. Your fame will be great.' Then the youths smiled and their mothers (wept/rejoiced).

Deywokleves's horses' necks were long. Deywokleves praised them: 'Swift two horses, bring me the strangers' herds/enclosures and carry me home alive. If I die, do not leave my body to the dogs.' Then he stood on the chariot. Then the two horses, bowing their heads, ran toward the strangers. They carried him home alive in the evening, and he gave them water and fodder.

Hsugenhes rushed at the house of Duskleves and followed (?). 'Your men killed my brother. Give me a hundred cows in exchange for him, or we will come with (weapons?).' Duskleves said: 'I owe you nothing. Your brother came as a thief into my field. He was stealing my cattle and died.' Hsugenhes reddened. Now the gods see what is true. Duskleves's own people left him(?) and Duskleves trembled in his heart. His people led a hundred sheep to Hsugenhes's house in the morning. Hsugenhes took them and did not come with (weapons). A knowing man took the sheep; he did not take the blood.

Hyudhsmos recognized/met a shepherd driving many oxen to the house. The house was far. 'Who is the master of these oxen?' The shepherd answered: 'Their master is king of the whole(?) people.' 'Where are you driving them?' 'I drive them to the river; they are thirsty.' Hyudhsmos said: 'Give me ten oxen and go.' The shepherd followed. The king's men come to the house. Then Hyudhsmos saw them and left. The shepherd smiled and gave them water.
uncertain: sokʷéyet 'followed' odd as reply to demand
